title: AUA 2026 Guideline on BPH/LUTS: Expanded Procedural Options
breakthrough: The American Urological Association published a multi-part guideline on management of lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia, with Part III covering procedural and surgical management. Prostatic artery embolisation was UPGRADED from Grade C to Grade B evidence and established as a legitimate option for prostates of 50 cc or more, including patients on anticoagulation at higher bleeding risk from conventional surgery. Aquablation evidence was extended into the 80–150 mL range. Intraprostatic drug-coated balloon may be offered for prostates of 20–80 cc with a prostatic urethral length of 32–55 mm and no obstructing median lobe. Separately, the EAU upgraded Aquablation to a strong recommendation as an alternative to TURP in moderate-to-severe BPH symptoms in March 2026.
impact: The large prostate has been the limiting case for minimally invasive options, pushing patients toward open or endoscopic enucleation. Extending Aquablation to 150 mL and legitimising embolisation above 50 cc changes what can be offered before that point.
practical: The drug-coated balloon indication is worth memorising precisely, because it is unusually specific: 20–80 cc, prostatic urethral length 32–55 mm, no obstructing median lobe. Those criteria require measurement, not estimation, and a patient with a median lobe is excluded regardless of size. Prostatic artery embolisation at Grade B is most valuable in exactly the patient who is a poor surgical candidate — on anticoagulation, high bleeding risk — which is a different selection logic from choosing it for a large gland alone, and it is delivered by interventional radiology, so the referral pathway has to exist. AUA and EAU now agree on Aquablation's standing, which makes it easier to defend.
link: Management of lower urinary tract symptoms attributed to benign prostatic hyperplasia: AUA guideline (2026) Part III: procedural/surgical management

verify.status: matched with corrections — every substantive change verified, one count dropped
verify.note: Verified against the published guideline (J Urol 2026, 10.1097/JU.0000000000005099, Part III): PAE upgraded from Grade C to Grade B for prostates ≥50 cc including anticoagulated patients at higher bleeding risk; Aquablation evidence extended to the 80–150 mL range; intraprostatic drug-coated balloon offerable for 20–80 cc with prostatic urethral length 32–55 mm and no obstructing median lobe; three-part structure. EAU independently upgraded Aquablation to a strong recommendation in March 2026. The submission was accurate on the substance — PAE to Grade B, Aquablation to 150 mL up from 80 mL, incorporation of drug-coated balloons, and the three-part format. Corrections: the '62 recommendations' count could not be verified and has been dropped; the DCB anatomical criteria have been ADDED, since the submission mentioned the device without its indication, and those criteria are the entire clinical content of a device recommendation; and the submission's claim about 'endorsing dual combination medical therapies (such as tadalafil with alpha-blockers or 5-ARIs)' could not be verified in Part III (which covers procedural/surgical management) and has been left out rather than asserted from the wrong part of the guideline.

title: POTOMAC: Durvalumab Plus BCG in BCG-Naive High-Risk NMIBC
breakthrough: POTOMAC randomised 1,018 patients with high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer after TURBT, 1:1:1, to intravenous durvalumab plus BCG induction and maintenance, durvalumab plus BCG induction only, or BCG induction and maintenance alone. At a median 60.7 months, durvalumab plus BCG induction and maintenance significantly improved disease-free survival — 67 events (20%) versus 98 (29%), HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.50–0.93), P=.0154, a 32% reduction in risk of high-risk recurrence or death. Median disease-free survival was not reached in either arm. Grade 3 or 4 treatment-related adverse events occurred in 21% of the durvalumab plus BCG induction and maintenance group, 15% with induction only, and 4% with BCG alone. No treatment-related adverse events led to death. The FDA has approved durvalumab plus BCG for BCG-naive high-risk NMIBC.
impact: It brings systemic checkpoint inhibition forward into BCG-NAIVE disease, where BCG alone already works for many patients — a different proposition from the BCG-unresponsive setting, and the first randomised evidence that adding it improves disease-free survival.
practical: The toxicity figures are what make this a decision rather than an upgrade: grade 3–4 treatment-related events rose from 4% with BCG alone to 21% with durvalumab plus BCG — roughly a five-fold increase — in a population where most patients would do well on BCG alone and where the endpoint gained is disease-free survival, not overall survival. Median DFS was not reached in either arm, so the absolute benefit is a 9-percentage-point difference in event rates at five years. The third arm is informative: durvalumab plus BCG INDUCTION ONLY did not carry the benefit, so maintenance is part of the regimen. Select for genuinely high-risk features and discuss immune-related toxicity explicitly before starting.
link: Durvalumab in combination with BCG for BCG-naive, high-risk, non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (POTOMAC): final analysis of a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial

verify.status: matched with corrections — hazard ratio exact, forum wrong, and a five-fold toxicity increase was omitted
verify.note: Verified: POTOMAC, Lancet 2025 (PubMed 41115436), 1,018 patients randomised 1:1:1, median follow-up 60.7 months, DFS HR 0.68 (0.50–0.93), P=.0154, 32% risk reduction, 67 (20%) versus 98 (29%) DFS events, median DFS not reached in either arm; FDA approved. The submission's HR and 32% figure are exactly right. Corrections. (1) FORUM: the submission says 'Five-year follow-up results presented at AUA 2026'; the final analysis was presented at ESMO 2025 and published in The Lancet. (2) TOXICITY OMITTED: grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were 21% with durvalumab plus BCG induction and maintenance versus 4% with BCG alone. In a BCG-NAIVE population — most of whom do well on BCG — a five-fold increase in serious treatment-related toxicity for a disease-free survival gain is the central trade-off, and the submission did not mention toxicity at all. Restored. (3) The submission omits the third arm's result: induction-only durvalumab did not carry the benefit, which makes maintenance part of the regimen rather than optional. (4) 'Positions systemic chemo-immunotherapy combination protocols as a potential front-line standard' overstates — this is checkpoint inhibition with BCG, not chemo-immunotherapy, and FDA approval is stated in place of a guideline claim.

title: PRIMARY2: PSMA PET-CT Halves Biopsies in Men With Equivocal MRI
breakthrough: PRIMARY2 was a multicentre, NON-INFERIORITY, phase 3 randomised trial at seven Australian sites in 660 biopsy-naive men with PSA below 20 ng/mL and either PI-RADS 3 or PI-RADS 2 with high clinical risk. Men were randomised to 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET-CT of the pelvis (n=331) or standard systematic transperineal biopsy of at least 12 cores (n=329); in the PET arm only those with positive PRIMARY scores of 3–5 underwent targeted biopsy, and those scoring 1–2 skipped biopsy altogether. Detection of clinically significant prostate cancer was 39 of 331 (12%) in the PET arm against 51 of 329 (16%) in the control — NON-INFERIOR, not superior. Biopsy was avoided in 163 of 331 (49%). Diagnoses of clinically INSIGNIFICANT cancer fell substantially, 14% versus 32%.
impact: The achievement is halving the biopsy rate and cutting overdiagnosis of insignificant cancer by more than half, while not missing more significant cancer than systematic biopsy would have found. That is a de-escalation result, and it is a strong one.
practical: Be precise about the direction of effect, because it is the opposite of what an enthusiastic reading suggests: clinically significant cancer detection was numerically LOWER in the PSMA-PET arm (12% versus 16%) and the trial was designed and powered as NON-INFERIORITY. PSMA-PET did not find cancer that MRI missed — it identified men in whom biopsy could be safely deferred. Sell it to a patient on that basis: a 49% chance of avoiding a transperineal biopsy and a much lower chance of being diagnosed with a cancer that never needed treating. The eligible group is narrow and specific — biopsy-naive, PSA under 20, PI-RADS 3 or high-risk PI-RADS 2 — and a negative PRIMARY score is a reason to defer biopsy under continued surveillance, not to discharge.
link: Effect of [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET-CT in the diagnosis of prostate cancer in men with equivocal or clinically high-risk non-suspicious findings on multiparametric MRI (PRIMARY2)

verify.status: REVERSED — a non-inferiority de-escalation trial was submitted as improving cancer detection
verify.note: The trial is real and important: PRIMARY2, Lancet Oncology 2026, 660 men at seven Australian sites, PSA <20, PI-RADS 3 or high-clinical-risk PI-RADS 2, randomised to 68Ga-PSMA-11 PET-CT (n=331) versus systematic transperineal biopsy ≥12 cores (n=329). The submission states that 'PSMA PET/CT SIGNIFICANTLY IMPROVED THE DETECTION of clinically significant prostate cancer (ISUP ≥2) while reducing non-essential prostate biopsies'. The first half is backwards. This was a NON-INFERIORITY trial and csPCa detection was NUMERICALLY LOWER in the PET arm — 39/331 (12%) versus 51/329 (16%) — meeting non-inferiority, not superiority. The submission repeats the error in its practical section, claiming PSMA-PET catches 'occult, aggressive lesions that standard MRI misses'; the trial shows no such thing. What it does show, and what the submission understated: biopsy avoided in 49% of the PET arm, and clinically insignificant cancer diagnoses cut from 32% to 14%. Entry rewritten around the de-escalation result, which is the genuine finding and a strong one. Also corrected: the submission dates it to EAU 2026 presentation only; it is published in Lancet Oncology. Added that a negative PRIMARY score means deferred biopsy under surveillance, not discharge.

title: Ten-Year Outcomes of Focal HIFU and Cryotherapy: HEAT and ICE Registries
breakthrough: An updated analysis of the prospectively maintained UK HEAT and ICE registries covered 3,477 patients with non-metastatic prostate cancer treated by primary focal high-intensity focused ultrasound (n=2,897) or cryotherapy (n=580) across 14 UK centres between 2004 and 2024. At ten years, prostate cancer-specific mortality was 0.13% (95% CI 0.027–0.45%), metastases 3.3% (2.1–4.9%) and all-cause mortality 12% (8.8–15%). The cohort was not low-risk: by EAU criteria 48% had favourable intermediate-risk, 23% unfavourable intermediate-risk and 25% HIGH-RISK disease.
impact: It is the largest and longest focal therapy dataset available, and the ten-year cancer-specific mortality and metastasis figures are low in a cohort a quarter of whom had high-risk disease. That is the strongest long-term evidence focal therapy has.
practical: It is a registry without a comparator, so the numbers cannot be read as equivalence to prostatectomy or radiotherapy — no radical treatment arm was followed alongside. Note the relationship between the figures: 0.13% prostate cancer-specific mortality against 12% all-cause mortality at ten years means these men were roughly ninety times more likely to die of something else, which tells you as much about who was selected and treated as about the treatment. Read it as evidence that focal therapy does not appear to cost men their cancer outcomes in appropriately selected disease, delivered at centres doing this routinely — and as a reason to discuss it, with the absence of a randomised comparison stated. Focal therapy requires a defined MRI-visible index lesion, systematic mapping to exclude significant disease elsewhere, and committed post-treatment surveillance including re-biopsy; without those it is not the treatment that produced these numbers.
link: Oncological outcomes following focal HIFU and cryotherapy for treatment of nonmetastatic prostate cancer in the United Kingdom: an updated analysis of 3477 patients from the prospective HEAT and ICE registries

verify.status: matched with corrections — figures exact, but a registry was framed as establishing equivalence
verify.note: Verified precisely: European Urology, published 11 July 2026, 3,477 patients (2,897 focal HIFU, 580 cryotherapy), 14 UK centres, 2004–2024; ten-year prostate cancer-specific mortality 0.13% and metastases 3.3%. The submission's '99.87% prostate cancer-specific survival (mortality 0.13%)' and '10-year metastasis-free rate of 96.7%' are both exactly right — they are the same published figures stated as complements. Corrections are about interpretation. (1) The submission says the data support recognition of focal therapy 'as a primary organ-preserving treatment option ALONGSIDE radical prostatectomy and radiation' and 'VALIDATES sub-total organ ablation as a SAFE ALTERNATIVE'. This is a registry with NO COMPARATOR ARM; it cannot establish equivalence to radical treatment, and 0.13% cancer-specific mortality against 12% all-cause mortality at ten years indicates strong competing-risk and selection effects that a single-arm cohort cannot separate from treatment effect. Both figures are now stated together so the reader can see it. (2) The submission omits the risk composition — 25% of this cohort had HIGH-RISK disease by EAU criteria, which strengthens rather than weakens the result and belongs in the entry. (3) Added the prerequisites (MRI-visible index lesion, systematic mapping, surveillance with re-biopsy), because the outcomes came from centres applying them and the entry as submitted implied the technique alone produces the result.

title: Extended Versus Limited Pelvic Lymph Node Dissection at Radical Prostatectomy
breakthrough: Two randomised trials address whether extending the nodal dissection helps. A phase 3 trial randomised 300 patients with intermediate- or high-risk disease to limited (obturator) or extended (obturator, external iliac, internal iliac, common iliac, presacral) dissection and found extended removal did NOT reduce biochemical recurrence. A larger trial cluster-randomised surgeons for 1,432 patients to limited (external iliac) or extended (external iliac, obturator, hypogastric) dissection; with longer follow-up it again found no difference in biochemical recurrence, but did find a statistically significant protective effect of extended dissection against METASTASIS, particularly distant metastasis.
impact: Biochemical recurrence — the endpoint the field used for years — is where extended dissection has repeatedly failed to show benefit. The signal that has emerged with longer follow-up is on metastasis, which is a harder and more meaningful endpoint.
practical: Do not justify an extended dissection on biochemical recurrence; two randomised trials have looked and not found it there. The defensible argument is the metastasis signal in the larger trial plus the staging information, weighed against the real morbidity — lymphocele, lymphoedema, obturator nerve injury, longer operating time. The templates in the two trials differ from each other and from what many surgeons call 'extended', so define what is being removed rather than relying on the label. And note the design of the larger trial: surgeons were cluster-randomised, meaning it tested a surgeon's habitual practice rather than a per-patient decision, which is arguably closer to how the choice is actually made.
link: Pelvic lymph node dissection in prostate cancer: update from a randomized clinical trial of limited versus extended dissection

verify.status: REVERSED — biochemical recurrence is precisely the endpoint where no benefit was shown
verify.note: The randomised evidence exists but says nearly the opposite of the submission. The submission claims over-10-year data 'revealed that while extended pelvic lymph node dissection showed no benefit in unselected patients, it provided a SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENT IN BIOCHEMICAL RECURRENCE-FREE SURVIVAL and delayed secondary systemic therapy in men with ISUP Grade Group 3–5 prostate cancer'. The published results: the 300-patient phase 3 trial (Eur Urol 2020) found extended PLND did NOT reduce biochemical recurrence; the 1,432-patient cluster-randomised trial (Eur Urol 2024 update) again found NO difference in biochemical recurrence, and the benefit that did emerge with longer follow-up was against METASTASIS, particularly distant metastasis. So the endpoint the submission credits with the benefit is the one where both trials were negative, and the endpoint where a benefit was found is not mentioned. The ISUP 3–5 subgroup specificity and the 'delayed secondary systemic therapy' claim could not be verified and have been removed. Entry rewritten with both trials, their differing templates, and the morbidity that has to be weighed. Added that the larger trial cluster-randomised SURGEONS, not patients, which changes how its result should be read.

title: LEGEND: Detalimogene Voraplasmid (EG-70) Non-Viral Gene Therapy in NMIBC
breakthrough: EG-70 (detalimogene voraplasmid) is a non-integrating, non-viral gene therapy given intravesically, carrying a plasmid that simultaneously expresses interleukin-12 and regulators of RIG-I to stimulate a local antitumour immune response in the bladder. In the phase 1 portion of LEGEND (NCT04752722) the overall complete response rate was 73% in NMIBC with carcinoma in situ. Preliminary phase 2 results in cohort 1 gave an overall complete response rate of 71% (15/21), 67% (14/21) at three months and 47% (8/17) at six months. The commonest treatment-related adverse events were dysuria (21.4%), bladder spasm (19.0%), urinary frequency (11.9%) and fatigue (11.9%).
impact: A non-viral, non-integrating platform avoids the manufacturing, handling and integration concerns that come with viral vectors, and it is administered in the office. In BCG-unresponsive CIS, where the alternative for many patients is cystectomy, another mechanistic class is worth having.
practical: The number that governs the conversation is 47% complete response at six months, not the 71% at any time — response attrition between three and six months is steep, and the six-month figure rests on 17 evaluable patients. This is phase 1/2 data in small cohorts, which places it well behind TAR-200 and cretostimogene, both of which have registrational or phase 3 data with two-year durability in the same indication. The tolerability profile is genuinely favourable — the reported events are local and low-grade. Treat it as a trial option and a mechanism to watch rather than a therapy to offer, and be careful not to present early complete response rates from small phase 2 cohorts as equivalent to the durability data now available for other agents.
link: Preliminary results from LEGEND: a phase 2 study of detalimogene voraplasmid (EG-70) in BCG-unresponsive NMIBC with CIS

verify.status: matched with corrections — trial real, phase misstated, and the durability drop-off was omitted
verify.note: Verified: LEGEND (NCT04752722), detalimogene voraplasmid / EG-70, non-integrating non-viral intravesical gene therapy expressing IL-12 and RIG-I regulators; phase 1 overall CR 73%; phase 2 cohort 1 preliminary CR 71% (15/21), 67% at 3 months, 47% (8/17) at 6 months; commonest TRAEs dysuria, bladder spasm, frequency, fatigue. The submission's mechanism description is accurate. Corrections. (1) PHASE: the submission calls it the 'Phase II LEGEND Trial'; it is a phase 1/2 study. (2) FORUM: 'presented during the opening plenary at AUA 2026' could not be verified; the documented presentations are ASCO GU 2025 and AUA 2024. (3) DURABILITY: the submission says only that EG-70 'achieved high complete response rates'. The published sequence is 71% at any time falling to 47% at six months on 17 evaluable patients, and in an indication where the alternative is cystectomy, the six-month figure is the one that matters. Restored, along with the comparison to TAR-200 and cretostimogene, which have far more mature data in the same population — the submission presented EG-70 as an established 'key bladder-preserving class' in AUA and EAU guidelines, which it is not.

title: Break Wave Lithotripsy: FDA-Cleared Anesthesia-Free Stone Fragmentation
breakthrough: SonoMotion's Break Wave device received FDA 510(k) clearance on 21 January 2026 for treatment of kidney stones. It uses LOW-PRESSURE FOCUSED ULTRASOUND — burst wave lithotripsy — to create standing stress waves within a stone under real-time ultrasound guidance, fragmenting stones in the kidney or ureter in fully awake patients without anaesthesia, at any site of care. The S.O.U.N.D. pivotal trial ran at 10 US and Canadian sites: adults with ureteral or renal stones of 4–10 mm underwent a 30-minute session entirely outside the operating room without anaesthesia or sedation. Of 64 treated patients, 94% of procedures were completed in clinic settings. The trial met all pivotal non-inferiority endpoints for safety and effectiveness. 97% of patients said they would choose Break Wave again for a future stone, including those with prior ureteroscopy or shock wave lithotripsy.
impact: Stone treatment without anaesthesia, sedation or an operating room removes most of what makes a stone episode disruptive — patients can drive themselves, eat beforehand, and return to work the same day.
practical: Note the cleared population: stones of 4–10 mm. This does not replace ureteroscopy for a large or complex stone burden, and the pivotal trial was 64 patients meeting NON-INFERIORITY endpoints, so it establishes acceptability rather than superiority. The mechanism is low-pressure focused ultrasound, not conventional shock wave lithotripsy — different physics, different acoustic requirements, and it needs an ultrasound window to the stone, so body habitus and stone position will exclude some patients. Real-time ultrasound guidance means the operator's imaging skill is part of the treatment. The strongest signal in the data is the patient-reported one: 97% would choose it again, including patients who had previously had ureteroscopy or SWL and therefore had something to compare it with.
link: Break Wave lithotripsy: FDA-cleared, anesthesia-free point-of-care technology (S.O.U.N.D. pivotal trial)

verify.status: matched with corrections — clearance and trial verified, mechanism and stone size clarified
verify.note: Verified: SonoMotion Break Wave, FDA 510(k) clearance 21 January 2026; S.O.U.N.D. pivotal trial at 10 US and Canadian sites, 64 patients, ureteral or renal stones 4–10 mm, 30-minute sessions with no anaesthesia or sedation, 94% completed in clinic, all pivotal non-inferiority endpoints met, 97% would choose it again. The submission's core claims — FDA-cleared, no general anaesthesia, no sedation, no post-procedural stenting, office-based — are accurate. Corrections. (1) MECHANISM: the submission calls it 'focused SHOCKWAVE technology'; it is LOW-PRESSURE FOCUSED ULTRASOUND (burst wave lithotripsy) creating standing stress waves — a materially different mechanism from shock wave lithotripsy, and the distinction determines the acoustic-window constraint. (2) SIZE: 'small-to-moderate ureteral and renal calculi' is replaced with the cleared 4–10 mm range, since that is what bounds the indication. (3) The submission claims it 'prompts revisions in endourology practice guidelines'; no guideline revision could be verified, and FDA clearance is stated instead. Added the 64-patient non-inferiority design and the acoustic-window/operator-skill constraints the submission did not mention.

title: ZIRCON: 89Zr-Girentuximab PET-CT for Indeterminate Renal Masses
breakthrough: ZIRCON was a prospective, open-label, multicentre phase 3 trial at 36 hospitals and practices across nine countries in patients with an indeterminate renal mass of 7 cm or less (cT1) suspicious for clear cell renal cell carcinoma and scheduled for nephrectomy. A single intravenous dose of [89Zr]Zr-girentuximab — an antibody targeting carbonic anhydrase IX — was followed by abdominal PET-CT five days later. Mean sensitivity was 85.5% (95% CI 81.5–89.6) and mean specificity 87.0% (81.0–93.1), meeting the primary endpoint. Mean positive predictive value was 92.9% (90.2–95.7), mean NEGATIVE predictive value 75.2% (71.2–79.3) and mean accuracy 86.0% (85.0–87.0). No safety signals were observed.
impact: A non-invasive test that identifies clear cell renal cell carcinoma with 92.9% positive predictive value can confirm a diagnosis that otherwise requires biopsy or resection — genuinely useful in the small renal mass where the differential includes oncocytoma.
practical: The negative predictive value is 75.2%, and that is the number that limits the use the submission promised. A NEGATIVE scan leaves roughly one in four patients with clear cell carcinoma — so it does NOT reliably exclude malignancy and cannot on its own justify abandoning surgery or surveillance for a suspicious mass. Use it the way its performance supports: a positive result confirms ccRCC with high confidence and can spare a biopsy; a negative result reduces but does not eliminate the probability, and the mass still needs a plan. The protocol requires a five-day interval between injection and imaging, which is a real scheduling constraint, and the trial population was cT1 masses of 7 cm or less scheduled for nephrectomy — performance outside that group is unknown.
link: [89Zr]Zr-girentuximab for PET–CT imaging of clear-cell renal cell carcinoma: a prospective, open-label, multicentre, phase 3 trial

verify.status: matched with corrections — trial verified, but the omitted negative predictive value undercuts the claimed use
verify.note: Verified: ZIRCON, Lancet Oncology 2024, prospective open-label multicentre phase 3, 36 sites across nine countries, indeterminate cT1 renal masses ≤7 cm scheduled for nephrectomy, sensitivity 85.5%, specificity 87.0%, PPV 92.9%, NPV 75.2%, accuracy 86.0%, no safety signals. Corrections. (1) The submission names it 'ZIRCON-X' and dates the evidence to EAU 2026; the pivotal trial is ZIRCON (2024), and 'ZIRCON-X' as a trial name could not be verified — real-world experience presented at EAU 2026 is plausible but is not the source of the performance data. (2) The clinically decisive omission: the submission says the test lets urologists 'differentiate BENIGN renal lesions (like oncocytomas) from aggressive ccRCC non-invasively' and would 'reduce diagnostic renal mass biopsies and unnecessary PARTIAL NEPHRECTOMIES for benign lesions'. That is a rule-OUT use, and the NPV is only 75.2% — about one in four patients with a negative scan still has clear cell carcinoma. The test's strength is rule-IN (PPV 92.9%), and the entry has been rewritten around that asymmetry, since acting on a negative scan is where a patient would be harmed. Added the five-day injection-to-imaging interval and the cT1 ≤7 cm population limit.

title: EAU 2026 Guidelines on Urological Infections: Fungal UTI and Non-Antibiotic Cystitis Therapy
breakthrough: The 2026 EAU Urological Infections guidelines are a limited update incorporating 36 additional studies across two sections. A NEW section 3.17 covers the diagnosis and treatment of fungal urinary tract infections. Section 3.18.3 updates periprocedural antibiotic prophylaxis for prostate biopsy, with growing support for the transperineal approach often WITHOUT prophylaxis. And the guidelines record that herbal therapy with Centaurii herba, Levistici radix and Rosmarini folium (BNO 1045) is NON-INFERIOR to fosfomycin trometamol in acute uncomplicated cystitis — between days 1 and 38, 238 of 285 (83.5%) in the BNO 1045 group and 272 (89.8%) on fosfomycin required no additional antibiotics. The stated overall focus is reducing unnecessary antibiotic use while maintaining effective, patient-centred care.
impact: Two antibiotic-sparing moves in one document: transperineal biopsy often needs no prophylaxis at all, and a non-antibiotic option is non-inferior for uncomplicated cystitis. Post-biopsy sepsis and fluoroquinolone exposure are the harms those changes address.
practical: The transperineal point is the one that changes a list: the route matters more than the antibiotic, and moving from transrectal to transperineal biopsy reduces infection to the point where prophylaxis is often unnecessary. That is a service-design decision — local anaesthetic transperineal capability — not a prescribing one. On BNO 1045, non-inferior is not equivalent: 83.5% versus 89.8% needed no further antibiotics, so roughly one in sixteen more patients on the herbal preparation went on to require an antibiotic anyway. That is an acceptable trade for antibiotic stewardship in uncomplicated cystitis in a patient who can be followed, and it is not an option for pyelonephritis, a complicated UTI or pregnancy. Fungal UTI now has a dedicated section — read it before treating candiduria, which is more often colonisation than infection.

verify.status: matched with corrections — all three substantive changes verified, scope narrowed
verify.note: Verified against the 2026 EAU Urological Infections guidelines and their summary of changes: a new Section 3.17 on diagnosis and treatment of fungal urinary tract infection; updated evidence and recommendations on periprocedural antibiotic prophylaxis for prostate biopsy in Section 3.18.3 with growing support for transperineal biopsy often without prophylaxis; and BNO 1045 (Centaurii herba, Levistici radix, Rosmarini folium) non-inferior to fosfomycin trometamol in acute lower cystitis, with 83.5% versus 89.8% requiring no additional antibiotics between days 1 and 38. The submission was accurate on all three, including naming BNO 1045 correctly — notable, since an obscure-sounding herbal product code is exactly the kind of detail this review has wrongly doubted before. Corrections: the submission describes a wholesale release that 'establishes international standards' for three domains; the 2026 document is a LIMITED update adding 36 studies across two sections, and that has been stated. Added the actual non-inferiority figures — the submission gave none, and 'non-antibiotic treatment works' reads differently against 83.5% versus 89.8% — plus the exclusions (pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, pregnancy) and the point that candiduria is usually colonisation.

title: ctDNA and Urine Tumor DNA in Upper Tract Urothelial Carcinoma
breakthrough: Paired circulating and urine tumour DNA are being evaluated as minimal residual disease markers in upper tract urothelial carcinoma. In a cohort monitoring both, baseline positivity was 69.2% for ctDNA and 88.9% for utDNA, falling to 46.2% and 21.4% respectively one month after surgery and before adjuvant therapy; the preliminary conclusion was that combined ctDNA and utDNA detection can serve as predictive biomarkers for recurrence and for adjuvant therapy efficacy. Separately, plasma ctDNA detected BEFORE extirpative surgery was highly predictive of muscle-invasive or non-organ-confined disease and strongly prognostic for progression-free and cancer-specific survival. CURATE-UTUC (NCT05595408), a multicentre prospective longitudinal cohort, is RECRUITING and has not reported.
impact: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma is usually diagnosed late, and preoperative staging is notoriously unreliable — which is why the preoperative ctDNA finding is arguably the more immediately useful one: it identifies muscle-invasive or non-organ-confined disease before the kidney comes out.
practical: The preoperative application is where a marker could change a decision now. If plasma ctDNA identifies likely muscle-invasive disease before nephroureterectomy, that is the patient for whom neoadjuvant chemotherapy should be considered — and it has to be considered BEFORE surgery, because removing the kidney removes the renal function that makes cisplatin possible. That single sequencing problem is the strongest argument for a preoperative staging biomarker in this disease. The postoperative MRD application remains investigational: no trial has shown that acting on a ctDNA or utDNA result after nephroureterectomy improves outcomes, and CURATE-UTUC has not reported. Note that utDNA positivity is higher than ctDNA at baseline and falls further after surgery, which is what you would expect from a marker shed directly into the urinary tract.
link: Circulating and urine tumor DNA dynamics predict minimal residual disease and recurrence risk in locally advanced upper tract urothelial carcinoma (CURATE-UTUC)

verify.status: NOT FOUND as cited — CURATE-UTUC is recruiting and has not reported; rebuilt on published cohort data
verify.note: CURATE-UTUC is real (NCT05595408, multicentre prospective longitudinal cohort, RenJi Hospital) but its recruitment status as of December 2025 is RECRUITING and no results have been presented. The submission states that 'Results from the prospective multi-center CURATE-UTUC trial PRESENTED AT EAU 2026 SHOWED that longitudinal monitoring of paired urine tumor DNA and circulating tumor DNA RELIABLY IDENTIFIES minimal residual disease and PREDICTS RECURRENCE following radical nephroureterectomy.' No such presentation or result could be found — this is the third entry across the two urology lists reporting results from a trial that has not reported (with PROBE and WATER IV). Entry rebuilt on what is published: a cohort study reporting baseline ctDNA positivity 69.2% and utDNA 88.9% falling to 46.2% and 21.4% one month postoperatively, with combined detection described as PRELIMINARY predictive biomarkers; and a separate finding that PREOPERATIVE plasma ctDNA predicts muscle-invasive/non-organ-confined disease and is prognostic for progression-free and cancer-specific survival. The preoperative application has been foregrounded because it is better evidenced than the postoperative MRD use the submission described, and because it addresses the specific clinical trap in this disease — that nephroureterectomy removes the renal function cisplatin requires, so neoadjuvant decisions cannot be deferred. The submission's claim that this 'facilitates timely delivery of post-operative adjuvant therapies' is not supported by any reported trial.
